title: Of No Avail, in My Faith and My Belief
intro: Al-Ma'arri mourns Abu Hamza al-Hasan, a Hanafi jurist whom Ibn al-Adim identifies as a judge of Manbij. Before the friend is named in the twenty-third bayt, a dove calls, enemies succeed one another in the same grave, and two stars look down on generations of travellers. The poet brings the scholar's working hand into view as it dips a reed into ink, then speaks to him after the last visitor has gone. The consolation offered to his brother al-Muhassin and his sons reaches back to the question of what becomes of the living.

translation: Of no avail, in my faith and my belief,
are a mourner's wail and a singer's song.
1.sharh: The verdict comes before the sounds it concerns. Neither the mourner nor the singer can change what happens to the people listening.

translation: The sound of a death announcement, when weighed
against glad news, is much the same in every gathering.
2.sharh: He moves from a solitary voice to news brought before an assembly. Even the verb “weighed” runs across the break before the listener hears the other side of the comparison.

translation: Did that dove weep or did she sing
on the tip of her swaying branch?
3.sharh: The same call can be heard as grieving or singing. The swaying branch gives the ear an accompanying movement without settling which it is.

translation: Friend, our graves fill the open ground.
Where are the graves from the days of Ad?
4.sharh: Present graves already seem to fill the available ground. The vanished burial places of the people of Ad make that familiar sight suddenly difficult to account for.

translation: Tread lightly. I think the skin of the earth
is made of these bodies alone.
5.sharh: The earth has a skin. Once he imagines its dust as earlier bodies, the weight of an ordinary footstep becomes a matter of courtesy to the dead.

translation: It ill becomes us, however long the ages pass,
to hold our fathers and forefathers cheap.
6.sharh: Time can hide the identities of those underfoot. It does nothing to release the walker from the respect due to earlier generations.

translation: Walk on air if you can, gently,
without strutting over the remains of God's servants.
7.sharh: His impossible direction gives force to the one the walker can follow. Someone who cannot spare the dead a footstep can at least spare them a swagger.

translation: Many a grave has served as a grave over and over,
laughing at the crush of opposites.
8.sharh: The grave outlasts its successive occupants. It is given the laugh the buried antagonists might once have had at the idea of sharing anything.

translation: And many a buried body lies on another's remains
through the long course of ages upon ages.
9.sharh: The little word for “many a” still governs this line from the previous one. The poet now imagines the depth of the earth as well as the breadth of its graveyards.

translation: Ask those two stars near the pole what peoples they have known
and what lands they have seen.
10.sharh: Two long-enduring stars can be asked for the testimony the graves can no longer give. Their paired verbs let them stand together as witnesses.

translation: How many sunsets have they lived through,
lighting the way for a traveller in the dark.
11.sharh: The stars endure sunset after sunset. Against their span stands one night traveller with an immediate need for their light.

translation: Life is weariness, all of it. My only wonder
is at anyone who wants more.
12.sharh: Weariness is the first word heard, before the poet even names life. What still has the power to surprise him is the wish to go on having more of it.

translation: Grief in the hour of death is many times
the joy in the hour of birth.
13.sharh: Birth and death are allotted exactly one hour each in his reckoning. The feelings of the people at the bedside have very different weights.

translation: People were made to endure. Those go astray
who think that death is the end of them.
14.sharh: The poet distinguishes the ending of this life from the extinction of the person. The next line gives the journey on which that distinction depends.

translation: They are only carried from a dwelling of deeds
to a dwelling of misery or right guidance.
15.sharh: People can act in the first dwelling and meet the consequence in the second. The passive “are carried” leaves their departure beyond their control.

translation: To lie down in death is to sleep
and give the body rest. Life is like a sleepless night.
16.sharh: He specifies the body as the part that rests. The bed on which someone has died takes on the repose an insomniac spends the night seeking.

translation: Daughters of Hadil, mourn with me, or promise
a man with little consolation that you will.
17.sharh: He turns to the doves for company in mourning. Even a promise will do for a man who calls himself short of consolation.

translation: Go on, how admirable you are. You are the ones
who know how to keep faith with those you love.
18.sharh: The call he could not interpret at first has become something he asks to hear again. He chooses to understand its persistence as fidelity.

translation: You have never forgotten one who perished long ago,
gone even before Iyad perished.
19.sharh: The commentators recount a lost dove chick for which doves have called ever since. Iyad, an ancient people, supplies a measure of how far back that imagined loss goes.

translation: Yet I disapprove of what you have done
with those necklaces round your throats.
20.sharh: The rings round the birds' necks look like necklaces. He treats a feature of their plumage as a mourner's decision to come wearing jewellery.

translation: Put on mourning. Borrow, all of you,
black clothes from the shirt of night.
21.sharh: Night has a shirt from which an entire flock can take its mourning dress. The request answers the brightness of the doves' collars.

translation: Then sing at the mourning gatherings and lament
in sorrow with the shy young women.
22.sharh: Once dressed for the occasion, the birds can join the women. Singing and lamenting, the alternatives of the opening, now take place in the same breath.

translation: In penitent Abu Hamza time struck at
a man of judgement, a companion to moderation,
23.sharh: At last the dead man has a name. Time's blow reaches a whole succession of people in him, the man of judgement, the jurist, the preacher and the transmitter.

translation: and a jurist whose thought built up for al-Nu'man
what Ziyad's poetry could never build.
24.sharh: Two men share the name al-Nu'man. Abu Hamza's thinking honours the jurist Abu Hanifa more than the poet Ziyad's praise honoured his royal patron.

translation: Since his death the Iraqi yields to the Hijazi
with little dispute, easily led.
25.sharh: On al-Batalyawsi's reading, the Iraqi jurists have lost their best advocate. Al-Tabrizi instead hears a tribute to the clarity with which Abu Hamza settled differences between the schools.

translation: And a preacher who, if he stood among wild beasts,
would teach predators kindness to lambs,
26.sharh: The sentence about time's blow resumes. The preacher's eloquence is measured by the largest change of heart imaginable in his listeners.

translation: a transmitter of hadith whose known truthfulness
left no need to trace a chain of transmission.
27.sharh: The verb waits across the break for its subject, his reputation for truth. It is a personal tribute expressed in the technical language of tracing a report to its sources.

translation: He spent his life in devotion, seeking knowledge
by uncovering its sources and weighing them.
28.sharh: His scholarship consists of two operations, finding the source of a claim and testing it. This is the work behind the reputation praised a moment earlier.

translation: His hand drew from a well of glass,
with buckets of reed, water made of ink.
29.sharh: A reed pen goes down into the glass inkwell and comes up full. The word for its tips can also mean buckets, so the hand of the scholar makes the same movement as a water drawer's.

translation: His fingers would not touch red gold,
such was his indifference to acquiring it.
30.sharh: The hand just seen reaching for ink has no appetite for gold. Touch gives a scholar's scruple a visible and almost physical form.

translation: You two who cared for him, bid that man farewell.
Farewell is the least provision for the road.
31.sharh: Two attentive companions receive the first funeral instruction. Farewell becomes the smallest provision one might put into a departing traveller's hands.

translation: Wash him with tears, if tears can purify,
and bury him between my inmost breast and heart.
32.sharh: The wish borrows two acts from burial, washing and laying the body to rest. He even asks whether tears would qualify as pure water before imagining a grave in his breast.

translation: Give him shrouds of leaves from the Qur'an,
for he stands above the costliest woven cloaks.
33.sharh: The imagined shroud honours what the scholar spent his life reading. No splendid woven fabric could have that particular intimacy with him.

translation: Follow the bier with recitation and praise of God,
free of sobbing and the counting of his virtues.
34.sharh: The two men entrusted with the burial are told what the funeral should sound like. In place of the conventional list of a dead man’s merits he would hear scripture and praise of God.

translation: Grief that does no good, and labour
that brings none of the gain of labour.
35.sharh: The living can expend immense effort in grief. Repeating the word for effort where a result should come makes its futility audible.

translation: Often the inward ache of grief has driven a mourner
to something out of keeping with sound judgement.
36.sharh: It is grief that acts on the mourner. The person driven appears before the grief that drives him, and even the word for grief crosses the verse's central break.

translation: As when Solomon missed the prayer
and turned upon the necks of his horses.
37.sharh: Al-Ma'arri follows an interpretation in which Solomon, grieved at missing a prayer, strikes the horses. Al-Tabari also records a reading from Ibn Abbas in which Solomon strokes them out of affection, and prefers that reading.

translation: Yet humankind and jinn were made subject to him,
as the testimony of Sad attests.
38.sharh: Solomon's power gives weight to the example. Sad is the name of the Qur'anic sura invoked as witness to the prophet's story.

translation: Fearing treachery from men, he entrusted to the wind
a son to feed on the milk of returning rains.
39.sharh: Some commentators tell of Solomon giving his son to the wind for safekeeping. The rain becomes the child's milk. Al-Batalyawsi objects to this account, which supplies details beyond the Qur'anic verse.

translation: He sought to bring the child to safety, though certain
that death was lying in wait.
40.sharh: The father knows the limits of his power and still seeks protection for his child. Death is given the patience of someone waiting by the road.

translation: Death cast the boy beside the throne for him,
the mother of ruin, calamity's sister.
41.sharh: The boy returns lifeless to the throne. The agent who flings him there is named only at the end, in the shape of two old personifications of death and disaster.

translation: How do you fare in your lodging since we parted,
you who so well deserve a visit from me?
42.sharh: He speaks to his friend in the familiar language of calling on someone. Addressing the grave as a new lodging lets him make the visit he can no longer pay.

translation: The physician has admitted his helplessness over you.
The visitors' coming and going has ceased.
43.sharh: The sickroom empties in a precise order. First the doctor can do nothing, then the people who used to come back day after day cease to return.

translation: Hope for you is quite gone. The grieving man feels
there is no return until the Return.
44.sharh: The same Arabic word is heard twice. The ordinary return a friend longs for has to wait for the Return of the dead at the Resurrection.

translation: Those who kept watch about your sickbed have fallen asleep.
Alas for the eyes of the sleepers.
45.sharh: Those tired eyes can at last close. His pity is for the sleepers, since the event that allowed them to rest was the death of the person they tended.

translation: You come of a family who went their way undeceived
by a life that keeps many lovers.
46.sharh: The line draws on an old word for a woman with several lovers. Abu Hamza's family understood that the favours life granted them were never theirs alone.

translation: May the earth leave you all unchanged. Lie within it
like swords within their sheaths.
47.sharh: The address widens to the family. A sheath conceals a blade while keeping it intact, a mourner's wish for the bodies concealed by earth.

translation: It grieves me that the passing nights should mingle
your crumbling foot bones with those of necks.
48.sharh: The nights carry on the work of decay. The distinction between the highest and lowest parts of a body disappears in dust, bringing the opening vision of the earth close to home.

translation: You were youth's close friend. When youth decided
to leave, you agreed to go along.
49.sharh: Youth is a friend with a decision to make. Instead of staying behind when that companion leaves, Abu Hamza dies with his youth still about him.

translation: You counted loyalty to your first companion
among the ways of a generous, noble man.
50.sharh: The friend of the previous line is youth itself. An early death can thus be imagined as an act of loyalty quite in character for the man they have lost.

translation: You took youth off while it was fresh. I wish
you had worn it out among men your age.
51.sharh: The garment still has years of wear in it. Wishing his friend could have worn it out breaks through the composed account of loyalty he has just offered.

translation: Go, then, you two, the best of those who go, deserving
rain clouds that come at evening and morning,
52.sharh: Both the young man and his youth depart. The old prayer for rain on a grave becomes a blessing for two, and the sentence has one more gift to give them.

translation: and elegies which, if they were tears,
would wash the lines away as they were recited.
53.sharh: The elegies depend on “deserving” in the previous line. If their grief became liquid, the poet would lose the very lines he was reading aloud.

translation: Saturn, highest of the planets in its dwelling,
has an appointment to meet death.
54.sharh: In the old planetary order Saturn occupied the outermost sphere of the planets. Distance from earth gives it no exemption from death.

translation: For the fire of Mars the accidents of time
hold an extinguisher, however high it blazes.
55.sharh: The red light of Mars becomes an actual fire in his imagination. Time can extinguish even so bright and distant a flame.

translation: The Pleiades depend upon their gathering together
until they too are counted as single stars.
56.sharh: It is the cluster that gives the Pleiades their identity. Once its stars are counted singly, the sky itself offers the bereaved family a likeness of dispersal.

translation: May al-Muhassin have a long span of life,
to the spite of every envious nose.
57.sharh: The surviving brother is now addressed by name. The wish for many years gives the household a future after the preceding images of universal loss.

translation: May he find some peace over his brother, and so may
his brother's sons, wounded to the liver.
58.sharh: The brother's sons share in the wish for consolation. The wound is in their livers, the traditional seat of a pain felt deep in the body.

translation: If the sea ebbs away from me before I drink my fill,
storing little pools will never quench my thirst.
59.sharh: Having tried to console the family, he admits his own deprivation. Someone who has lost a whole sea cannot make up the loss by putting away little quantities of water.

translation: Every house is bound for ruin, the one a grey dove builds
and the chief's house with its high tent pole.
60.sharh: Nest and great tent come under the same word for a dwelling. The dove whose voice began the poem returns as a builder whose home also has to fall.

translation: Man is a traveller. The shade of a lote tree spares him
the trouble of pitching ropes and pegs.
61.sharh: If a traveller is going on shortly, a tree already provides what he needs. The labour of putting up a tent gives a practical measure for a human lifetime.

translation: God's decree is plain, yet people differ,
one calling others astray, another showing the way.
62.sharh: The divine decree is set beside human disagreement about its meaning. Al-Khwarazmi connects the division to disagreement over the return of the dead.

translation: What has bewildered all creation is this,
a living being newly made from lifeless matter.
63.sharh: Al-Batalyawsi asks how the soul brings a body to life. Al-Khwarazmi hears a question about resurrection, how a body reduced to remains can live again.

translation: The wise, the truly wise, are those undeceived
by a coming-to-be whose end is decay.
64.sharh: The repeated word “wise” holds the listener before the final test of wisdom. Coming to be and passing into decay supply the last pair in a poem that began with two human sounds.

1.1.2.meaning: Of use, capable of bringing a benefit.

1.2.5.head: شادٍ
1.2.5.meaning: A singer who lifts the voice in song.

2.1.3.head: النَّعِيّ
2.1.3.meaning: The announcement of a death or the person bringing it.

2.2.6.head: نادٍ
2.2.6.meaning: An assembly or the place where it meets.

3.2.5.head: مَيّاد
3.2.5.meaning: Swaying repeatedly, here of a branch.

4.1.1.head: صاحِب
4.1.1.meaning: Friend or companion, shortened here in direct address.

4.1.5.head: الرُّحب
4.1.5.meaning: The breadth of the earth. The word finishes on the first consonant of the next half.

4.2.6.head: عاد
4.2.6.meaning: Ad, an ancient Arabian people whose destruction the Qur'an recounts.

5.1.2.head: الوَطء
5.1.2.meaning: The pressure of a foot on the ground.

5.1.5.head: أَديم
5.1.5.meaning: Skin or hide, here the earth's upper surface.

6.1.4.meaning: To have grown distant in time. Al-Tamimi's text has “was far removed”.

7.1.3.head: اِسطاعَ
7.1.3.meaning: You were able, a shorter form of the ordinary verb for being able.

7.2.4-5.head: رُفات العِباد
7.2.4-5.meaning: “The crumbled remains of God's servants.” Al-Tamimi has “the necks of enemies” and records “the necks of God's servants” as well.

8.1.2.head: لَحد
8.1.2.meaning: A niche dug into the side of a grave to receive the body.

9.2.3.head: الأَزمان
9.2.3.meaning: Ages, plural. Al-Tamimi's excerpt uses the singular “time”.

10.1.2.head: الفَرقَدان
10.1.2.meaning: Al-Farqadan, the Two Calves. Kochab and Pherkad are neighbours of the Pole Star in the Little Bear. They stay in the northern sky as the traveller makes his way by night.

10.2.3.head: آنَسَ
10.2.3.meaning: To descry something, make it out.

11.1.4.head: زَوال
11.1.4.meaning: The daylight's passing. Al-Batalyawsi's witness has “the light of day”.

11.2.2.head: مُدلِج
11.2.2.meaning: A traveller who takes the road by night.

13.1.5.head: المَوت
13.1.5.meaning: Death. The commentaries print “loss” and explicitly record “death” as a variant.

14.2.3.head: النَّفاد
14.2.3.meaning: Exhaustion or extinction, as when a supply runs out.

15.2.4.head: شِقوَة
15.2.4.meaning: Misery, here one's lot in the life to come.

16.2.5.head: السُّهاد
16.2.5.meaning: Sleeplessness, the inability to take one's rest.

17.1.1-2.head: بَنات الهَديل
17.1.1-2.meaning: “Daughters of Hadil”, the doves. Hadil is the lost chick of an old story and a word for a dove's cooing.

17.1.3.meaning: Join someone in mourning, as one lamenting woman supports another.

18.1.1.meaning: Go on, let me hear more of the sound already begun.

18.1.2-3.meaning: “How admirable you are”, a conventional expression of praise.

18.2.3.head: أَحسَنَ
18.2.3.meaning: They know well how. A transmitted alternative addresses the birds directly as “you”.

19.2.1.head: الخالي
19.2.1.meaning: Gone by, describing an age long past. The final long vowel is shortened.

19.2.6.head: إِياد
19.2.6.meaning: Iyad, an early Arab tribal group whose passing is a measure of antiquity here.

20.2.4.head: جيد
20.2.4.meaning: The neck, especially as the place a necklace is worn.

21.1.1.head: تَسَلَّبنَ
21.1.1.meaning: Lay aside your finery and put on mourning clothes.

22.2.4-5.head: الغَواني الخِراد
22.2.4-5.meaning: Beautiful, retiring young women. The second word stresses reserve or shyness.

23.1.4-5.head: أَبو حَمزَة
23.1.4-5.meaning: Abu Hamza al-Hasan ibn Abi Husayn, a Hanafi jurist, hadith transmitter and judge of Manbij. Ibn al-Adim identifies him as the subject of this elegy.

23.1.6.head: الأَوّاب
23.1.6.meaning: One who repeatedly turns back to God. The word continues after the break.

23.2.2-3.meaning: “A possessor of judgement”, a man of good sense.

23.2.4-5.head: خِدن اِقتِصاد
23.2.4-5.meaning: “A companion to moderation”, someone for whom restraint is habitual.

24.1.4.head: النُّعمان
24.1.4.meaning: Al-Nu'man, the personal name of Abu Hanifa and also of the Lakhmid king praised by Ziyad. The name straddles the two halves.

24.2.6.head: زِياد
24.2.6.meaning: Ziyad ibn Mu'awiya, the poet al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, who praised al-Nu'man of al-Hira.

25.1.1.head: العِراقيّ
25.1.1.meaning: The Iraqi jurist stands here for the Hanafi school.

25.2.4-5.head: سَهل القِياد
25.2.4-5.meaning: “Easy to lead”, yielding readily in a dispute.

26.2.2.head: ضارِيَة
26.2.2.meaning: A beast habituated to hunting prey.

26.2.4.head: النِّقاد
26.2.4.meaning: Young sheep or lambs, the natural prey of the predators.

27.1.4.head: أَحوَجَ
27.1.4.meaning: To put someone in need of something. Its delayed subject is his known truthfulness.

27.2.5.head: الإِسناد
27.2.5.meaning: Isnad, the chain of named transmitters through whom a report is traced.

28.1.3.head: ناسِك
28.1.3.meaning: A devout person leading a life of restraint.

29.1.4.head: قَليب
29.1.4.meaning: A well, here the glass inkwell into which he dips.

29.2.1-2.head: غُروب اليَراع
29.2.1-2.meaning: “Tips of the reeds.” Ghurub also denotes large buckets, making the pen a water drawer's tool.

30.2.4.head: العَسجَد
30.2.4.meaning: Gold, here gold he could have acquired.

31.1.3.head: حَفِيّ
31.1.3.meaning: Attentive and solicitous. Two such companions are addressed.

32.1.5.head: طُهر
32.1.5.meaning: What can serve for purification, here for washing the dead.

32.2.3.meaning: The body's inmost parts, imagined here as a chamber of the breast.

33.1.1.head: اُحبُ
33.1.1.meaning: Give as an honouring gift. The two companions are to give the dead man his shroud.

33.2.5.head: بُرد
33.2.5.meaning: A woven mantle or wrap, sometimes of costly cloth.

34.1.1.head: اُتلُ
34.1.1.meaning: Follow the bier, addressed to the two burial attendants. The dual is utluwa. The mention of the Qur’an also recalls the verb’s other meaning, to recite.

34.2.4.head: التَّعداد
34.2.4.meaning: The ritual listing of the dead person's virtues in a lament.

35.1.1.head: أَسَف
35.1.1.meaning: Grief. The isolated sound can suggest ‘asf, harsh treatment. Both continuous transcriptions give asaf, the grief named in both diwans and taken up in the next line.

35.2.4.head: غَناء
35.2.4.meaning: Benefit or avail. The similar word for singing begins with a different vowel.

36.1.4-5.head: جَوى الحُزن
36.1.4-5.meaning: “The inward ache of grief.” The last word continues across the break. A variant has “bereavement”.

37.1.5.head: سُلَيمان
37.1.5.meaning: Solomon, son of David. The horses appear in Qur'an 38, verses 31–33. His name continues across the break.

37.2.2.head: أَنحى
37.2.2.meaning: To turn upon something and strike it.

38.2.6.head: صاد
38.2.6.meaning: Sad, the thirty-eighth sura of the Qur'an, which mentions the horses and a body upon Solomon's throne.

39.2.2.head: سَليل
39.2.2.meaning: An offspring or son, here the child in the commentators' account.

39.2.4-5.head: دَرّ العِهاد
39.2.4-5.meaning: “The milk of the returning rains.” One shower follows another like successive feeds.

41.2.2-3.head: أُمّ اللُّهَيم
41.2.2-3.meaning: Umm al-Luhaym, a name for death as a devourer. She is the subject of “cast”.

41.2.4-5.head: أُخت النَّآد
41.2.4-5.meaning: “Sister of calamity”, a second name for death.

42.2.5.head: اِفتِقاد
42.2.5.meaning: Seeking someone out to see how they are. The reciter and the commentary text have iftiqad. The Beirut edition has intiqad, closer scrutiny, a reading also reported by al-Batalyawsi.

43.2.3.head: العُوّاد
43.2.3.meaning: People who call on a sick person.

44.1.5.head: الواجِد
44.1.5.meaning: The grieving man. The word crosses the break. The compact Beirut text has “grief felt that there was no return”.

44.2.4.head: مَعاد
44.2.4.meaning: An ordinary return, such as a friend coming home.

45.1.1.meaning: To fall asleep. The same verb can mean to keep vigil, the Beirut edition’s gloss. The commentators explain that his attendants finally slept when they lost hope for him.

45.2.4.head: الهُجّاد
45.2.4.meaning: Sleepers, here those who once kept watch by the bed.

46.1.3.head: أُسرَة
46.1.3.meaning: Family or kin. Al-Batalyawsi's text has “company, people”.

46.2.4-5.head: ذات ضِماد
46.2.4-5.meaning: “A woman with several lovers”, an old expression for the inconstancy of the life that courts us.

47.1.3.head: الصَّعيد
47.1.3.meaning: The earth's surface or soil, here the soil of burial.

48.2.4.meaning: Necks, the high part of the body opposite the feet.

49.1.2-3.head: خِلّ الصِّبا
49.1.2-3.meaning: “Youth’s close friend.” The commentaries also give khidn, another word for an intimate. One continuous transcription gives safa, affection, but the other gives “youth”, the companion addressed with Abu Hamza at 52.

51.2.4.head: الأَنداد
51.2.4.meaning: His peers, the people of his own generation.

52.2.3-4.head: رَوائِح وَغَواد
52.2.3-4.meaning: “Evening and morning rains”, a traditional blessing for a grave.

53.1.1.head: مَراثٍ
53.1.1.meaning: Elegies, governed with the preceding rain by “deserving of”. The isolated clip suggests marrat, “times”. Both continuous transcriptions give marath, the poems whose tears could wash away their lines.

54.1.1.head: زُحَل
54.1.1.meaning: Saturn, the outermost of the planets in the old geocentric order.

55.1.2.head: المِرّيخ
55.1.2.meaning: Mars, whose red appearance supplies the image of a fire.

55.1.4.head: حَدَثان
55.1.4.meaning: The changes and calamities time brings.

56.1.1.head: الثُّرَيّا
56.1.1.meaning: The Pleiades, a compact cluster of stars visible to the unaided eye.

56.1.3.head: اِجتِماع
56.1.3.meaning: Gathering together. The compact Beirut edition instead reads “through the parting of the company”.

57.1.2.head: المُحَسِّن
57.1.2.meaning: Al-Muhassin, Abu Hamza's brother, identified by the commentators and in al-Tamimi's biography.

57.2.2-3.head: رَغماً لِآنُف
57.2.2-3.meaning: “Dust to their noses”, an expression of humiliation or frustrated envy.

58.2.3-4.head: جَرائِح الأَكباد
58.2.3-4.meaning: “Wounded in their livers”, describing the sons in their grief. A witness to al-Batalyawsi reads qara’ih, also suggesting wounds.

59.1.3.meaning: To subside or drain away, said of water.

59.2.5.head: الثِّماد
59.2.5.meaning: Little stores of water, here set beside a sea.

60.1.6.head: الوَرقاء
60.1.6.meaning: A grey dove. The word ends in the second half.

60.2.3-4.head: رَفيع العِماد
60.2.3-4.meaning: “High of tent pole”, a description of a chief's standing.

61.1.2.head: ظاعِن
61.1.2.meaning: A traveller who will soon break camp.

61.2.1.head: السِّدر
61.2.1.meaning: Lote trees, whose shade shelters a traveller. The article falls in the first half.

61.2.3-4.head: الأَطناب وَالأَوتاد
61.2.3-4.meaning: Tent ropes and the pegs that anchor them.

63.2.1.head: حَيَوان
63.2.1.meaning: A living, sentient being, including a human being.

63.2.2.head: مُستَحدَث
63.2.2.meaning: Newly brought into being. The Beirut note takes Adam’s creation from earth as its example. Al-Khwarazmi understands the raising of bodies from their remains.

64.2.2.head: كَون
64.2.2.meaning: Coming into being, paired with decay or dissolution.

64.2.4.head: فَساد
64.2.4.meaning: Dissolution. The recitation and the edited commentaries end with indefinite fasad. The Beirut edition and the Tanwir commentary give the noun its definite article.
